HAvRE, JAM 2S, 1869.
The steamship Pereire Captain Duchesne sailed
from Havre Friday, the 18th inst, for New York,
touching at Brest which port she LEFT the day fol-
lowing, the 10th. She experienced strong head
winds and heavy weather almost from the start.
The storm increased In violence until, when i've
days out from Brest, it became q furious
gale which threatened the destruction Of the
ship. Heavy seas broke over her, carrying
away entlrely her forward deck cabin, the dining
saloon for the second class passengers deluging the
engine room and partially disabling the ship. The
storm caused the vessel to lurch tremendously and
the passengers and crew were thrown from place to
place with great Violence The loss Of life and in
Jury to person on board are attributable to this
cause only.


At length on the 21st instant the Perere shipped
an immense sea, estimated at 1000 tons which COM
pletely flooded the cabin and killed one Of the pas
sengers outright-a Miss Funckelburg, from Ger
many.


The storm coming from the west Captain Du-
chesne doubtful OF his ability to safely ride it out
thought 1t prudent to put the vessel about, which
was done, and she arrived safely at Havre on the
2eth instant.


As before stated three of the crew and three of
the second class passengers were killed ana many
others injured. The injuries, however, were mainly
slight and all are now dong well. Mr.. Callighan,
Catholic priest, Mr.. Foulquier Frenchman, and
Miss Funckeburg were the only passengers killed.
The latter had her neck broken. None Of the first
class passengers were injured.


The Pereire's passengers VIII 60 forward to New
York in the ST. Laurent next Saturday Before the
arrival Of the Pereire at Havre the passengers
bled in the cab and unanimously passed resolutions
complimenting the commander OF the steamship.
Captain Duchesne, for his courage and seamanship
a. demonstrated not only by the present case, but
many times before, and especially in the collision
OF the vesJa with the Arctic on the American coast
years ago.

PROVIDENCE, Sept. 9--The gale last evening
from four to live O'Clock was the most severe known
here since 1915, when the city was partially sub
merged. Throughout this State the damage is i'm
mense, and several lives have been lost. In this
city the Hartford Railroad depot was demolished,
and Rose & Walkers tannery partially blown
down. The Oriental mill was unroOfed, and two
operatives badly hurt. The Chestnut street church
steeple was blown down, and nearly all the other
church steeples were injured.


Probably one hundred buildings were unroOfed
The Bristol Railroad will not be passable for
raj days. Many vessels are ashore in Narragansett
and Mount Hope bays, but most of them will come
of without much damage. small new church on
Narragansett pier was entirely demolished. The
sloOp Resolution went to pieces in Wexford harbor
and two men were lost. Octavian Rice was killed
in his barn in Warwick.


Great damage is reported in Bristol, East Green
wich, Newport, Pawtucket, Fail River and other
places


The papers of to-day contain four or five columns
of details OF the wreck and ruin by the storm.


The hurricane of last night extended over most
of eastern Massachusetts At Nahant large
dwelling and stable were blown down. and the
depot on the steamboat wharf was blown into the
sea. At Hull every boat at anchor in the harbOr
was driven ashore or sunk. The windows of the
Marion House were blown in and the Outbuildings
unTooted. At bingham the streets were blocked
with trees, and barns and chimneys were blown
down. The Agricultural Hall at Marshfield was
levellcd to the ground. In Abingdon three church
steepes tell, and the large nail and tack factory in
South Arlington was unrooied.


At Braintree the steeple of the Congregational
church was carried OFF.


At Newburyport, and towns further east, the gale
was less violent.


The Coliseum organ is ruined. 1t had just been
sold to Chicago parties for $4,000. The big drum
was also smashed.


Nearly every vessel in Boston harbor dragged
anchor and many collided sustaining damage.


AT Marblehead Frank Barrett, of Nashua, n. H..
was killed.


The Sycamore House, on Nantucket Beach, was
swept from its foundation but the inmates were
unDjured, having Just left for safer quarters.


The gale all along the eastern coast was the most
terrific experienced for years.


Captain Smith, of the schooner j. T. Knight
has been held in $4,000 bail for trial. charged with
casting away his vessel. The mate has been dis
charged.

The Wilmington Commercial of last evening
contains the following news:-


The fire at Delaware City, on Tuesday evening,
proves not to have been of incendiary origin, as
was at first supposed 1t resulted from the fall
of a lamp which was hanging in the stable.
There were several drivers in the stable at the
time and, on the discovery of the fire, they in-
mediately gave each other the alarm, and all
sprang from the windows except one, who,
thinking they were only awaking him to fool
him, lay still until it was too late for escape.
He was q well-known character about the town
- known almost entirely by the name of
"Jimmy"-and was n driver on the canal The
number of mules destroyed was forty. There
were also eight tons of hay and some feed in the
stable, which were also consumed.


The fire at one time assumed threatening pro-
portions, and it was only with the greatest diff
Guilty that the extensive carriage making shop of
Jesse Alexander could be prevented from catch
ing fire. The stable of Major j. b. Henry did
catch fire several times, but the flames were
suppressed each time and the building thus saved.


The sight next morning was most sickening,
the bodies of the animals being strewn amongst
the ruins. The body of Jimmy" the driver,
was not found until some search had been made,
and it was horrible sight, nothing being left
but the blackened trunk, his legs arms, and
head having been burned entirely off


A Noble Deed-The HerOism of n Lame Boy.


The Commercial also says:-


On Monday last a young boy, son of Mrs.
Forest living on Riddles Banks, near this city,
had occasion to take his aunt across the dam of
Jessup d Moore's paper mills, to the east side of
the Brandywine creek. On returning, owing to
the strong wind and high freshet, the boat be-
came unmanageable and was carried over the
dam breast. Providentially, the boat, as it was
rushing down the rapid water below the dam,
struck upon the only rock in the creek
whose top was above the water, and here
young Forest scrambled and thereby was
saved from immediate drowning. The
people soon gathered for the rescue, but the
question arose as to how the boy was to be saved
from his perilous condition. At that moment a
lame boy, with crutch, came forward and said,
jected, until his father, Patrick Murien, who
was present, said LET him go: you can't drown
that boy" A rope was procured, and young
Mulrien, with rope and crutch, went to the
rescue. After feeling the water a little, he
threw the crutch ashore, and manfully plunged
into the rapid, rushing flood of waters,
headed for the rock in the middle of the
creek, where sat the half-drowned, chilled, and
frightened boy. Mulrien swan round and
round till he got through the eddying water,
and on to the lee side of the rock, where
he scrambled up; tied his rope around
young Forest, and with his feet had to push him
off the rock into the seething, boiling current
the boy stubbornly refused to leave the only
place of safety, being benumbed with cold, and
afraid to face the dangers of the rapid flood
again. The man soon pulled him ashore where
kind hands ministered to his wants. The
trouble then was how Mulrien was to get back
again, as he still sat upon the rock and looked
quietly at the people, then at the rushing flood
He prepared himself for the plunge, and, after
circling round the partly covered dangerous
rocks, directed his course down the creek, made
headway with the current, and very soon gained
the shore, some distance below the scene of the
disaster.

The facetious Dana inclines to the idea that
George Francis Train knocked the bottom out
of the democratic tub in Connecticut in rally
ing the Fenians against English and company
as bloated bondholders, English aristocrats
and Tammany Hall tricksters. But this
explanation will do only for the marines.
Greeley thinks that the democrats recoiled in
renegades, Dixon and Babcock, and that this
Johnson leaven leavened the whole lump
and upset English; but this is shallow solu-
ton. Yet, again, while we are told by Brick
Pomeroy that it was the joint stock coalition
against the New Haven democratic ''ring" that
settled their hash, another expounder says it
was the temperance people rallying against the
grogshops and another that Jewell, the re-
publican candidate for Governor, being jewel
to the liquor people, they rallied round him
and carried him in. Finally, we are informed
that Father Carmody, Catholic priest of New
Haven, shocked at the democratic perjuries
coming to his knowledge last November, de-
nounced this immortality in the late canvass,
and thus turned the tide against the party.


None of these explanations, nor all of them
together, meet the case. They are only the
straws in the current The democracy Of Con-
necticut, with the party generally elsewhere,
were knocked in the head by the Tammany
Convention of last July. The Tammany ticket
of Seymour and Blair and the Tammany plat
form, against General Grant, did the business
for Connecticut last November, and these late
results are but reaffirmation Of that popular
verdict, negro question and all. In word, the
democratic party, on its old issues and old party
dogmas, is defunct, and it needs some new and
powerful galvanic batteries to bring it into life
again. English has only been the last to go
out with the ebb tide.

New YORK, July 31.-About dusk last evening
whole family, consisting of a man, wife, and
two daughters, about fifteen and seventeen years
of age, and two little children, were observed
rowing in North river in small boat. When
opposite Bulls ferry the boat capsized and the
whole party appeared to have been thrown into
the water. Two men Immediately put out to
their rescue, but before they could reach the
party the man, woman, and two eldest daughters
sank.


The two little ones, however, were found in
the boat, which had righted, but was half full of
water They were rescued and brought to the
shore. Both were too young to give their names,
and the men who rescued them were unable to
ascertain the name of the family. One of the
little girls could only say mamma" and papa"
They were safely cared for, and this morning
an effort is being made to find out their names
1t is reported that the parties resided on the
brow of the hill at the upper end of Hoboken,
and the husband is druggist doing business in
Brooklyn.

The public will receive with satisfaction the
announcement that Gen. Butterfeld's resig-
nation has been accepted, and success
sor appointed. The vacation of his Office
by the General has not been awaited with that
feverish impotence which some of the com
ments in the public journals would indicate; but
it's nevertheless true that so long as the General
remained in office, a profound sense of dis
trust pervaded the business community. Let
us trust that ex-senator FOlger, who succeeds to
the Office, and that all subsequent appointees
who may in other years and under other
Administrations succeed him, will not
fail to profit by the lesson which Gen.
ButteTfeld's career so pungenty en-
forces. The man who holds position
of this delicacy and responsibility must not
only be free from evil, but even from the sus-
picion of evil The Sub. Treasurer in New York
must neither speculate with the Government
money, nor speculate in Government securi-
ties with his own money during the term of
his office He must be content with the legiti-
mate income of his position, and abstain from
any business interests that might in any way
affect it.

In descanting upon the Queens speech
the London Times hits upon an idea which
is not quite new to us, for we have felt
its force, and more than once gave utterance
to it, namely, that the telegraphic communi-
cations established between foreign nations
must partially supersede or render unneces-
sary the formal establishments of our foreign
missions, with all their ceremony, diplomacy,
gold lace, dress swords, cooked hats and other
expensive and ridiculous paraphernalia. When
governments are brought within few min
utes' speaking distance Of each other ambassa-
dors and ministers plenipotentiary become very
like puppets. What the Times says is this =
''That the Queens opening and closing
speeches are apparently inconsistent, but the
explanation is found in the fact that the inter-
national relations depend on the reciprocity of
the feelings OF the people and not on the nego-
tiations of their ministers. Messrs. Johnson,
Stanley and Seward have been succeeded by
others, but the sureties of peace and friend
ship abide on stronger bases than diplomacy
can furnish" What the London paper means
is that these strong bases are our submarine
cables, which are multiplying so fast that
every government in the world will soon be in
direct communication and embassies will be-
come mere matter of form.

BY the brig Nautilus, Captain Turner, which ar

news is received by business house in this city of

the high seas. 1t brings to mind the fearful scenes
witnessed board the African slavers several years
ago, and surpasses any of the dark deeds on Ship
board that have been chronicled for a long time
Some two years ago the French barque Murialdi was
fitted up by the Tahiti Cotton Company, and sailed
for the Gilbert Islands, Auckland ostensbly on
trading expedition but really for the purpoSe of
securing cargo of Coolies, to be used as slaves on
the plantations She was provided with stocks
and arranged in all respects like SLAYER. She pro-
cured her human freight, and, after considerable
difficulty, succeeded in completing her voyage in
safety in spite Of the obstacles placed In her path
by the French Government and the natives. The
Muriad venture proved SO remuneratve that the
wait for the excitement to die out, before sending
for another cargo of coolies About six months ago
the cotton company purchased the barque Margaret
Bran6er, arranged her similar to the Muradi, and
sent her to the Gilbert Islands, under the Tahtian
flag, after more labOrers for their plantation. No
unusual precautions were taken in equpping the
vessel to enable the officers and crew to withstand
any outbreak which might take place, and the own
ers the gallant barque sail away with no appre-
hension that the voyage would result dsastrousy.
The Brander arrived at the Gilbert Islands in due
season, and Immediately set to work procuring the
"laborers" wanted. In doing this more trouble was
experienced than had been anticipated The natives
of the Gilbert Islands are fierce and revengeful and
are bitter in their hatred towards the whites. At
last, however, the complement was obtained, and
the vessel sailed away with three hundred men and





covered the destination of the Brander found that
they were to be subjected to slavery, and the Mu-
riadis cargo had been converted to that purpose.
Instantly they became suen and eyed their cap
tors with wicked look. Feeling somewhat inse-
cure, Captain Blackett, who had charge of
the vessel, ordered the strctest watch to be
kept of the movements made by the coolies,
and all possible precautions for the safety of the
vessel officers, and crew taken His fears We're not
groundless for when some two weeks out the coolies
rebelled in the night killed Captain Blackett, two of
the officers, and several men, and charged around
the vessel in the widest fury hacking their victims
in the most frightful manner While the poor
wretches were carrying on their horrible WORK of
mutating and disfguring their victims, the mate Of
the vessel managed to secrete himself below. His
absence was soon discovered, and the now half
craZed savages set TO work to discover his where
abouts. MIstrustng their intention, and with
presence of mind seldom equaed, he placed
keg OF powder under the main-hatch
and arranged fuse. Then calling out
to the coolies above he scampered back
from the powder as far as possible. When the fel-
lows had crowded around the hatchway and were
peerirg down to see him, he fired his fuse, and the
explosion which followed killed nearly all on board.
The rest so demoralized that they jumped
board, or fell easy victims TO the remorseless war
fare waged by the mate and the few remaining men.
Singular 1t may seem, the vessel not so badly
damaged that she would not ioat, and the mate
ceeded in bringing her back to Tahiti The Cotton
Company feel dissatisfied with their investment but
are not discouraged, and 1t Is currently reported

CLARKsvLLE, July 2S.-Last night the pas
senger train bound North, and due here at IS
A. NJ met with a terrible accident at Budd's
creek, about nine miles south of his place. 1t
appears that as the train was passing over the
trestle the structure gave way, precipitating the
engine, baggage-car, and two passenger-cars
into the creek.


The cars were smashed into fragments, and
being piled on top of each other, made it ex-
tremey difficult for the panc-stricken passen-
gers to extricate themselves from the debris
Immediately after the accident, and before the
extent of the disaster could be ascertained, the
ears caught fire either from the engine or the
oil used for Illuminating purposes, and burned
rapidly.


Those who escaped from injury succeeded in
dragging out the disabled, and, as far as known,
those who were killed. Among the latter are
Eugene Riley, the engineer; the fireman, whose
name is not known, and New Orleans cotton
merchant named Hugh Mccall.


About one hundred persons were wounded,
the following seriously:-Mr. Fountaine, wife.
three children, and servant of Memphis; Chas
Brown, baggage master; Walter Wilcox, of
Clarksville; Mr.. Stowe, of Eufaula Ala; Colonel
j. j. Buckende of the Patriot of this place:
Mr.. Dugan, express messenger; and Judge Caul-
kins, wife, and two children, of New Orleans.


Amongst those who are deserving of the
greatest credit for their heroic and humane as
sistance in caring for the wounded and admins
tering to their wants, are Mr.. Hamilton Pike,
son of General Albert Pike, Mr.. Sanger, and Mr..
Wood, of New Orleans, and Captain Lowe, the
conductor of the train. The cars were entirely
consumed.


This is the second time within three years that
this trestle-wOrk has given way and the officers
of the road are severely censured for their appa-
rent criminal negligence. 1t is feared that
several of those injured will not recover They
are all being cared for in the best possible
manner.

dross and let the light of heaven shine upon
code which is so pure that, after eighteen
hundred years, mankind stands only upon the
threshold of its beauties.


The coming Of Christ and the great law
which He set for human aims found the world


but poorly tuned for such harmony. Petty
nationalities, local prejudices, utter ignorance,
non-communication among States and bar


baric civilization, which made the word
stranger a death warrant, could not and did
not receive such teachings. Nor did Christ
expect they would. Could the human mind
at that date have reached and practised such
morality it would have been already perfect,
and the race would have had no need of a
long and magnificent upward struggle of
redemption such as it has labored through
in the preface of the past. Mankind,


however, started on its mission, but with
the idea that it was already fitted to appre-
ciate the highest morals taught by Christ


So dull was the human brain in that epoch,


and so little had the intellect been unrolled,
that the teachers Of the masses were obliged
termed faith, instead Of reason. The great
problem Of morals never was the simple enun-
citation of doctrines and Bible explanations.
1t was and is rather the fitting of humanity to
the appreciation and partial application Of a
code which we may always approach but never
reach


In the worlds history we have seen the
religion of Christ made political weapon by
the men who have ridden into temporal power
by assuming that the spiritual should control
all. Christ, however, was the first statesman
who clearly saw the evils of such union,Y
and said, ''Render to Caesar the things that are
Caesars, and to God the things that are Gods. I
The ambitious saw the splendid field open
to them, and commenced the task of
making grand spiritual and political mo-
nopoly. The Roman empire fell into their
hands and became unit of religious force,
which, through faith in the spiritual took
the form of force in the temporal, and
circled around the Mediterranean, form
ing great nationality whose particles
were held together by the central power
which infused itself through the mass
it tried to animate. But the world, despite
this, moved onward. The Roman built his
vast system of military roads, the soldier of
Iberia met the Syrian, the pillars Of Hercules
no longer marked the boundary Of the West,
the Gaul accompanied Caesar to Britain, man
looked at man, conversed with him, exchanged
ideas and grew civilized. There was improve
ment. Mankind had gained step, Christ was
was more appreciated. Now comes the inva-
sion Of Italy by that magnificent barbaric blood
of Northern and Eastern Europe. The hold
ers Of the spiritual power cling hard to their
position, and compact between vigorous
Goths and Vandals on the one side and the
tottering clergy on the other gives the latter
second lease Of life for dogmas, bishops and
Popedom. Out Of the ruins Of the Roman
empire nations are finally carved, and long,
black night called the middle ages follows as the
result of the attempt to force man in the wrong
direction. The Crusades come, and again the
world catches sight of the true Christ. Europe
awakes from her torpor, her armies cross the
country, man again meets man, and Palestine
becomes the touchstone of the modern march
to civilization.


Truly did the old Crusaders do q Christian
work, and the Sermon on the Mount was again
placed in the foreground. Again the world
began to progress the human brain expanded,
The wooden type was cut, and in that one in
vention the race saw more OF Christ than
Rome had been able to teach in the whole
fourteen centuries that preceded it. Reason
came to the rescue of man and the brain took
better and more moral poise. The man
IN all things began to live beyond

moral. Then came those
magnificent discoveries of Columbus Vasco
Ii Cana and Magellan. The awakening
brain of Europe leaped forward with all its
vigor to seize the prizes offered to those who
ire foremost in progress and its consequent
civilization. The discoveries demanded finer
md more accurate astronomy-demanded
arger ships, better roads for trade, greater
ecurity for international intercourse, more
Of each other and more inventions.

During the past week have met some of the

BAIT MORE, Oct. 4.-We have had another

Yesterday afternoon Officer Hale started from
Fitchburg with a fellow named Frank Francis
in charge, who had just been sentenced to the
State Prison for four years for pocket picking.
The convict was handcuffed, and sat in the
smoking car two seats from the door, the officer
sitting in the seat opposite him, and talking
with the conductor. All of a sudden Francis
started from his seat rushed to the door,
opened it, and jumped from the platform while
the cars were going at the rate of forty miles
an hour. The officer started and grabbed
him by the coat just as he jumped but his hold
failed and the fellow got away. The cars were
at once stopped and parties started in pursuit.
They found the bushes, and telegraph pole
where he jumped Off covered with blood, but
though they searched for hours they could not
find the prisoner. The place where he jumped
was near Lincoln, in the woods where there is
thick growth of underbush, in which he probably
secreted himself, The impression of those who
searched for him, judging from the blood
spilled, was that he was so badly injured that
he would not live. Warden Haynes offers $50
reward for his arrest.-BOStOn Journal

HARRISBURG, Aug. IA terrible accident

this city at 3'15 this morning. When the train
had reached point about nine miles north of
here, IL struck some large rocks which had fallen
upon the track from an overhanging embank-
ment and the engine, together with baggage
express cars, and one passenger car were thrown

headway at the time, the force of the concusson

names are not yet ascertained, were instantly
killed, and several other attaches of the train
severely injured.

were crushed into q complete mass of ruins A
portion OF the debris remained on the carriage
road adjoining the track, and the remainder
went into the canal below. The passenger car
was thrown on to a wall, on the other side of
which was a declivity of twenty feet Provi-
dcntially the car did not 90 over, and was only
saved by torn-up rail which had been thrown
over the wall, one end being driven into the
ground, whilst the other supported and saved
the tottcring car, which was full of passengers


The escape is one of the most miraculous on
record. Had the car gone over the WALL the
loss of life would have been fearful to contem-
plate. None would have escaped injury. While
the car was in this perilous position the passen-
gers all got out safely, not one being injured.

HARRISBURG, April 16.-The following is
summary of the condition of some of the most
important bills of the session on the day Of ad-
journment:-


The General Registry law, which includes
Philadelphia, has passed both houses.


The Cattle Market bill passed the Senate, but
was killed in the House.


The Revised Tax bill taxing coal, oil, and whisky
passed the House and was killed in the Senate.


The Adulteration of Drugs bill was killed in
the House Committee.


The bill giving salary to the Port Wardens
passed both houses The second Port Wardens'
bill giving them power to arrest captains, was
killed in the House. The Militia law, reducing
the tax from two dollars to fifty cents, was de-
feated in the Senate The Philadelphia Trust
bill, and the State Board of Public Charities,
passed both houses The bill eXempting sewing
machines of seamstresses from levy and sale
under execution for rent has passed both houses.


The bill taxing national banks and saving in
stitutious one per- cent on their capital, and ex-
empting them from all local taxation, passed
both houses


The salt-slush bill, preventing the sailing of
railroad tracks, has passed both houses.


Both Metropolitan police bills were killed by
the Senate, as was also the Metropolitan Tele-
graph bill.


The bill allowing parties to be witnesses in
their own cases has passed both houses.


The Broad street omnibus bill was killed in the
Senate.


The bill allowing members of Council to be
eligible to a position by resigning as Council
men has passed both houses.


The bill authorizing the Governor to commute
the death penalty was vetoed by the Governor.

in the House. The bill driving the farmers off
Second street was defeated in the House. The
bill dividing the Twentieth ward into two school
districts has passed both houses. The North
Penn Passenger Railway defeated in the
Senate The bill giving Penn Square to several
public institutions was defeated. The Park sup
plement passed both houses. The House of
Correction bill was killed in the Senate Com
mittee The bill regulating the fees of public
officers in Philadelphia was killed in the House.
The bill changing the Rule in ''Shelleys Case"
was defeated. The proposition to repeal all
laws exempting property from taxation was in
corporated in the general Tax bill and was of
course defeated. The bill requiring coal mines
to be ventilated passed both houses. The Cruelty
to Animals bill passed. The bill toseXempt the
Eleventh Street Opera House from general laws
securing the public from danger from fire was
defeated in the House.

scented to various bills passed during the session.

proceedings as unjust. and maintain that as the
British government had appropriated all the public
lands OF the island they should pay the Governors
salary.
